findings.title: Denial-cache keys collide for distinct name/folder pairs
findings.body: The key concatenates raw `name` and `parent` values with `_`, so distinct checks can produce the same key. For example, for the same namespace, user, and action, `name=dashboard_a,parent=folder` and `name=dashboard,parent=a_folder` both generate the same suffix. If the first check is denied, the second check will hit the entry at `Check` line 117 and be denied without evaluating its actual permissions. Dashboard and folder identifiers are not escaped or otherwise structurally encoded here. Use an unambiguous encoding (for example length-prefixed fields or a hash of a structured tuple).

findings.title: Negative authorization results remain effective after permissions change
findings.body: A denial-cache hit returns immediately before reading current permissions, but this cache is never invalidated when dashboard/folder permissions, roles, or folder inheritance change. Consequently, if a check is denied and the user is then granted access to that same resource (or a resource is deleted and recreated with the same UID), all checks for that tuple remain denied for `shortCacheTTL` despite the database now allowing access. This partially reintroduces the stale-denial behavior the permission requery is intended to avoid, including for newly created resources. Invalidate the negative entry on relevant writes or avoid using it when a newer permission/folder state may exist.

findings.title: Permission refresh still evaluates inherited access using a stale folder tree
findings.body: After a cached permission map does not authorize a resource, this path reloads permissions but calls `checkPermission` against the same `folderCache`. If the folder tree was cached before a child folder was created, a user with a scope on its parent will be denied access to a newly created dashboard in that child: `checkInheritedPermissions` cannot find the new child in the stale tree, even though the freshly loaded parent permission is sufficient. The resulting false denial is then itself placed in the denial cache. Refresh or invalidate the folder tree when retrying an inherited check after a cache-derived denial.

findings.title: Cache misses can trigger repeated permission queries despite singleflight
findings.body: The cache lookup was removed from `getUserPermissions`, leaving an unconditional database query inside `singleflight`. Concurrent requests can all miss `getCachedIdentityPermissions`; if one request populates `permCache` and another reaches `sf.Do` after that first singleflight call has completed, the latter starts a new database query instead of observing the newly populated cache. A burst of requests that passed the outer cache check before the first write can therefore issue multiple serial permission queries. Recheck `permCache` inside the singleflight callback (and likewise for anonymous permissions), or retain a cache check in these fetch methods.

findings.title: The denial-cache test passes even if the denial cache is not consulted
findings.body: The test claims to populate an allowing permission cache entry, but it stores `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. Without the denial-cache shortcut, `checkPermission` also denies this map and the fake store has no allowing permission, so the test still passes if the new denial-cache lookup is removed or broken. Store `true` for the dashboard scope and assert that no permission-store lookup occurs, so the test verifies that the explicit denial entry takes precedence.
